pr_body:
This PR implements `@ <timestamp>` modifier as per [this design doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uSbD3T2beM-iX4-Hp7V074bzBRiRNlqUdcWP6JTDQSs/edit#heading=h.pc8jkhltm231).

An example query: 
```
rate(process_cpu_seconds_total[1m]) 
  and
topk(7, rate(process_cpu_seconds_total[1h] @ 1234))
```
which ranks based on last 1h rate and w.r.t. unix timestamp `1234` but actually plots the 1m rate.

Closes #7903

This PR is to be followed up with an easier way to represent the start, end, range of a query in PromQL so that we could do `@ <end>`, `metric[<range>]` easily.

![Screenshot from 2020-10-28 19-02-17](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15064823/97442969-7242f180-1950-11eb-8f55-084eb4709f6a.png)

I think there are benefits in making the argument of `@` dynamic. 

For one, we probably want it to support an upcoming function `now()` to, for example, graph the top 10 fullest disk as of _now_. But that function's return value still won't depend on the evaluation time.

However, I can see MTD-like queries where I want it to depend on the evaluation time, e.g. where you want to compare a value at time _t_ to the value at the beginning of the month relative to _t_, i.e. something like `@ start_of_month(time())`. (The yet-to-be-created `start_of_month` function would probably take `time()` as the default, and of course there could be more elegant ways, referring to what I wrote about fields in a fully-fledged time struct.) This would allow error-budget burn graphs, which you want to reset at the beginning of a new billing period etc.

To make the latter work nicely, we probably want an `@`-style start of a range in a range selector. If we allowed dynamic ranges, it could look like `increase(errors_total[time()-start_of_month()])`, but an `@`-syntax could say "from then to the time of evaluation", i.e. `increase(errors_total[@start_of_month()])`. But I guess I'm digressing…

The final plug for a dynamic argument of `@` would be to retrieve it from recording rules or do arithmetic on it, which relates to my musings about timestamps and durations. 

See https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jMeDsLvDfO92Qnry_JLAXalvMRzMSB1sBr9V7LolpYM/edit#heading=h.vmb7pe7hp12
To be clear: The above are just musings, not concrete suggestions what to implement in this PR. I think this is great as a demo.
Yeah this prototype is just barebone stuff required for a PoC, other helpers like `now()` `end()` etc would be based on what we decide and I don't plan implementing in this PR yet.
Note that this PR constitutes a breaking change to PromQL, and thus should not be merged.
I see this as an incremental additional without breaking anything that exists right now. But anyway, should not be merged yes, just a PoC.

> Note that this PR constitutes a breaking change to PromQL, and thus should not be merged.

I agree with @codesome that it is not breaking anything from what I can see

It breaks the invariant that has existed for 5+ years that PromQL does not look into the future, and thus that no samples beyond the evaluation time of a query may be accessed. Users could be depending on this, thus it is a breaking change.

I am definitely in favor of this modifier, love it! Thanks, @codesome for this prototype. What I like about this syntax is that is quite clear. Sure, there is some boilerplate but it's fully understandable and does what expected.

> It breaks the invariant that has existed for 5+ years that PromQL does not look into the future, and thus that no samples beyond the evaluation time of a query may be accessed. Users could be depending on this, thus it is a breaking change.

Hm @brian-brazil  if that's the case isn't this as easy as returning an error when requested `@timestamps` is outside or requested range? :thinking:

> Users could be depending on this, thus it is a breaking change.

That's not the definition of a breaking change.

https://xkcd.com/1172/

> if that's the case isn't this as easy as returning an error when requested @timestamps is outside or requested range?

First of all, no, it's not the case. This is not a breaking change. Everything that works before will continue to work in exactly the same way.

Second, it is core to this feature that you @-request a timestamp from outside the queried range. For example, if you have a topk graph for the busiest CPUs over the last hour, and then you want to zoom in to look at a particular peak, you are now looking at a time interval in the past but still need to run the selecting query with the same fixed @-time. (This is BTW what most competing metrics systems get wrong with the "easy" task of displaying the top-5 busiest CPUs.)

> Hm @brian-brazil if that's the case isn't this as easy as returning an error when requested @timestamps is outside or requested range? thinking

That would cover it, as long as it's not after the start time it can't break anyone downstream due to this.

> Everything that works before will continue to work in exactly the same way.

I disagree. Anyone who depends on the not looking into the future invariant would be broken, and this is highly likely to affect at the least both explicit and implicit caching. We'd basically be asking for all users to audit all their uses of the API to see if this would impact on them, or any of their downstream users.

Just because something isn't an explicitly enumerated behaviour doesn't mean that we can change it without causing breakage.

Is anyone aware of any software relying this current behavior or is this a theoretical concern?

A feature flag which is on for PromCorThanos and off by default would solve this if anyone is aware of anyone needing opt-in.

Being theoretical is sufficient for it to be breaking. There's stuff I'd like to break that I'd expect to have zero real impact, but can't.

In terms of concrete examples the most obvious would be Trickster, but I expect this would impact on large chunks of the userbase causing non-obvious breakage. I imagine there's tons of scripts out there running queries over "past" data and caching/storing it somewhere, presuming that the query result can't change as new data comes in.

> A feature flag which is on for PromCorThanos and off by default would solve this if anyone is aware of anyone needing opt-in.

I don't think this is what you meant to write, as upgrading does not equate to opting in to breaking changes.

I feel we can discuss if it's breaking change or not in a different thread as this is not blocking this proposal as far as I get this, right? (: We expect the timestamp to be inside the queried range.

> Second, it is core to this feature that you @-request a timestamp from outside the queried range. For example, if you have a topk graph for the busiest CPUs over the last hour, and then you want to zoom in to look at a particular peak, you are now looking at a time interval in the past but still need to run the selecting query with the same fixed @-time. (This is BTW what most competing metrics systems get wrong with the "easy" task of displaying the top-5 busiest CPUs.)

> (Also, currently it only works with a timestamp, I will be adding support for `start()` `end()` soon)

do we want range() too ? `max_over_time(foo[range()]) @ end()`
Yes. I will add that too. (I had it in the doc, forgot the mention here. So `start()` `end()` and `range()` but _not_ `now()` is what I remember as what we decided).

>  So start() end() and range() but not now() is what I remember as what we decided).

We haven't decided anything here, beyond not having any form of now(). So whether these would be present nor a proposed syntax is not agreed.

> We haven't decided anything here

So let's decide now? I propose adding start() end() and range() which is not any form of now().

> > We haven't decided anything here
> 
> So let's decide now? I propose adding start() end() and range() which is not any form of now().

I second this. I wonder if the `()` are really needed.

> I wonder if the () are really needed.

If we remove it, they are valid metric names, hence can cause confusion. With (), we would be consistent with time().

> I propose adding start() end() and range()

First, what would range() be for an instant query? I don't think range() makes sense as a PromQL feature semantically. I also question what the use case is here. Why should the width of a graph affect the ranges of the rates within it?

Secondly that's a confusing syntax, as those look like functions but they aren't. That would make it look like you could use scalar expressions as ranges and timestamps - which you can't. Or that you can use them as part of expressions - which you can't. I think that any syntax here needs to make it really obvious that they are not scalar expressions.

Thirdly, these would break the current ability to take any PromQL query_range and evaluate one of its steps using the query endpoint by only adjusting the times. This could in particular cause issues for backfilling rules, and other places where you might shard a query across time to parallelise it

> If we remove it, they are valid metric names, hence can cause confusion. With (), we would be consistent with time().

Being consistent with time() is a problem, and being consistent with metric names is also a problem - as neither of those can go after an @.
Do we want to introduce some kind of templating then? `{start} {end} {range}`
Or `$start $end $range`

> > I propose adding start() end() and range()
> 
> First, what would range() be for an instant query? I don't think range() makes sense as a PromQL feature semantically. I also question what the use case is here. Why should the width of a graph affect the ranges of the rates within it?

Instant query is 0 as maxt-mint = 0

It is not for rates but more for the `topk_over_time @ end` case.

> Secondly that's a confusing syntax, as those look like functions but they aren't. That would make it look like you could use scalar expressions as ranges and timestamps - which you can't. Or that you can use them as part of expressions - which you can't. I think that any syntax here needs to make it really obvious that they are not scalar expressions.

> Do we want to introduce some kind of templating then? {start} {end} {range}
> Or $start $end $range

Those are possibilities, how would they interact with Grafana? Layering similar syntaxes across languages tends not to end well.

{start} looks like an (invalid) selector. $start looks like it could be used as a scalar expression.

> Instant query is 0 as maxt-mint = 0

That's a parse error, you can't have a zero range (and it wouldn't be of much use anyway). Therein lies the problem.

> Yes, hence juste @ end would be enough

`end` is a valid expression. It can't go after an @ for non-trivial semantic reasons, but most users wouldn't realise that.

> $start looks like it could be used as a scalar expression.

We define what `$` or anything else for that matter mean. I see these to be equivalent to pre-processing, so I don't see anything wrong with $end to be used in place of scalar expression as it would get reduced to a number before the query execution.

> > Yes, hence juste @ end would be enough
> 
> `end` is a valid expression. It can't go after an @ for non-trivial semantic reasons, but most users wouldn't realise that.

How is that different from `offset` being a valid expression ?

> How is that different from offset being a valid expression ?

It's a question of parsing. offset can only go after a selector, in all other cases it's a metric name. Here it's quite a bit more involved.

I'm expecting at some point that someone is going to propose allowing expressions after the @. Such expressions would have to quite restricted for semantic/performance reasons, however taking advantage that would be very confusing for users. For example `end` meaning one thing in what is nominally a PromQL expression and another in a part of PromQL expression would be confusing.
I don't get it, `offset` is also a valid selector (metric name)

> I don't get it, offset is also a valid selector (metric name)

`offset` always has type instant vector. If we go with what you're talking about, `start` could end up being either be a scalar or an instant vector depending on context. That sort of context-dependent typing is extremely challenging for users of a language to deal with, such as seen in Perl.

> We agreed during the dev summit that this is an experimental feature and the feeling I got was that some people would be ok to break that promise with @ end queries.

Thinking a bit, I'm not so sure. The base change proposed here means that trickster would have to update their code to deal with the new feature so their cache invalidation remains correct, but trickser can still cache these new queries.
If we add in start/end then trickster can no longer cache such queries in any useful way, as it's only safe to cache when start/end are identical - it can't use prior evaluations over other ranges to avoid recalculating things. That's quite a bit different, as that's preventing an entire class of performance optimisations that many users currently rely on.
You see `end` as a scalar/timestamp when I see it as a keyword.
I think that breaking trickster/caching was accepted because it would be disabled by default and that we could add additional caching headers to help them.

> You see end as a scalar/timestamp when I see it as a keyword.

That it's a keyword isn't relevant, the problem is that it would have a type. The other potential parsing of that token has a different type. So if I see the token `end` I can't know its type from local information, I'd have to potentially look at the broader query.

In the case of offset I only need to look forward a token to see if the next token is a duration.

> we could add additional caching headers to help them.

This is something different. My point is that cacheablitiy would be greatly diminished in practice, no matter what extra hints are sent back. A refresh of a graph pane always needs to reevaluate the entire range of the query. You could no longer re-use parts of results from previous queries using this feature, only entire other queries that have exactly the same start and end.

issue_context.title: topk/bottomk X over time, X = [avg, sum, min, max, etc...]
issue_context.body:
## Proposal
**Use case. Why is this important?**

Quoting [this comment](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/7878#issuecomment-686373735) here

> Another thing we cannot do natively in PromQL is graphing top N time series. All the details [are in this blog post](https://www.robustperception.io/graph-top-n-time-series-in-grafana).
> TL;DR is, if you use topk in query_range, you can get much more than k time series. We cannot graph just k metrics based on some condition (say sum, avg, etc is the highest for past x hours).
> While it can be done in Grafana, it would be nice to be able to do it natively in PromQL to write ad-hoc queries.

Implementing this would not be as simple as adding a new method because of the `query_range` semantics (it run's an instant query at all the timestamps in the range and is just a syntactic sugar over instant queries), as we need fixed set of metrics to be plotted for entire range.

I plan to work on a proposal to fix/implement this without breaking the `query_range` semantics and without needing invasive changes in PromQL. Please raise your concerns if any :)

Update: A clarification. The aim of this is to be able to do `topk X over time` where `X` can be average, sum, min, max, median, etc.

Uhm, timestamp is step invariant. It doesn't care what the evaluation time is.

`timestamp(timestamp(...))` is not step invariant because the timestamp of the result of the inner `timestamp(..)` depends on the eval time, hence affects the outer `timestamp(...)`. So while `timestamp(..)` itself is step invariant, nested timestamp() is not.

For that matter, I think `timestamp(...)` with anything not vector selector will not be step invariant.

> So while timestamp(..) itself is step invariant, nested timestamp() is not.

You're confusing a function being step invariant with an expression being step invariant. The timestamp function is step invariant, it never touches the evaluation time as it only looks at the samples being passed in to it.

> For that matter, I think timestamp(...) with anything not vector selector will not be step invariant.

No, timestamp() is always step invariant. If you're seeing otherwise, that's a bug in the engine somewhere as it means  samples in instant vectors have the wrong timestamp.
